canonical_topic: Hydrocarbon classification by carbon chain length
definition: Hydrocarbon fuels are categorized by the length of their carbon chain, notated Cn where n is the number of carbon atoms; chain length determines whether the fuel is a gas, liquid, or solid at standard temperature and pressure.
core_idea: Short carbon chains form natural gas (gaseous), mid-length chains form petroleum (liquid), and the longest chains form coal (solid).
key_points: Carbon-chain notation: capital C plus a subscript for the number of carbon atoms, e.g. C5 = five-carbon molecule.
Shortest chains (natural gases) are gaseous at standard temperature and pressure.

Even after processing, fuels remain mixtures of hydrocarbons of varying chain length rather than a single pure molecule — e.g. gasoline is predominantly C7–C11 but also contains some C5, C6, C12, C13, etc.

The proportion of lighter/heavier molecules in a fuel like gasoline can vary substantially, so the carbon-chain makeup of a named fuel (e.g. 'gasoline') may be defined slightly differently across countries, states, or even processing locations.
relationships: Carbon chain length is the underlying variable linking natural gas, petroleum, and coal as points on one spectrum rather than unrelated substances.
trading_implications: Because named fuel grades (e.g. gasoline) are regionally-defined mixtures rather than fixed chemical formulas, specification differences across jurisdictions can matter for physical delivery/quality contracts.
caveats: Natural gas, petroleum, and coal are not chemically distinct categories in an absolute sense — they are ranges along a continuous carbon-chain-length spectrum.
